conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling now that your baby has arrived. We’ll use a short questionnaire called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS). It’s simply ten questions about your mood, thoughts, and experiences over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers, and everything you share stays between us unless you or your baby’s safety is at immediate risk. My goal is to understand how you’re doing so we can make sure you have the support you need. Ready to begin?

First, I’d like to know: in the past week, have you still been able to enjoy things the way you used to, or has that sense of enjoyment slipped away?

Hi Sarah… I guess I’m ready.

Enjoyment? Honestly, most things feel kind of flat. I used to like going for coffee with friends or even just watching a show, but lately it feels like I’m doing them because I “should,” not because they make me happy. I still go through the motions, but the spark isn’t really there.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

I can still laugh sometimes—like if my partner makes a silly joke or the baby does something cute—but it feels kind of forced or short-lived. It’s not that natural, easy laughter I used to have. Most of the time I’m too tired or worried to find things genuinely funny.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. When I think about plans—even little things like taking the baby for a walk or having my mom visit—I mostly feel dread or nothing at all, instead of that little buzz of excitement I used to get. Everything just feels like another task on the list.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a lot. If the baby’s fussy, I immediately think it’s because I didn’t feed him right or I missed his sleepy cues. When I couldn’t get him to nap yesterday, I kept replaying every single thing I did wrong. My head tells me other new moms manage fine, so it must be my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be sitting there, baby’s asleep and safe, but my heart’s still racing and I’m scanning the room for things that could hurt him—outlets, blanket edges, the temperature. Sometimes there’s no real trigger at all; the worry just sits on my chest like a weight until I distract myself by cleaning or checking his breathing again.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes… a few times this week. Once, I was just warming a bottle and suddenly felt like I couldn’t breathe, like the walls were closing in. My hands were shaking and I had to put the baby in the crib so I could sit on the floor and try to calm down. There wasn’t anything dangerous happening—I knew that—but my body still felt like it was in danger.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, honestly. It feels like the minute I finish one feeding, the next is due, or there’s laundry piled up, or the dishes, and I can’t keep up. I’ll start one chore, hear the baby cry, drop everything to go to him, then come back and feel paralyzed looking at the mess. Sometimes I just sit there staring because I don’t know which thing to tackle first.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah. Even when the baby’s asleep, I lie there with my mind racing—did I burp him long enough, is he breathing, will I ever feel like myself again? Some nights it takes me an hour or more to drift off, and then I jolt awake at every tiny sound. It’s like I’m too tired to sleep, if that makes sense.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty often. I wake up most mornings feeling heavy, like there’s a gray cloud hanging over everything. Sometimes I’ll just look at the baby and feel guilty because I’m not bubbling over with joy like I thought I would be. The sadness comes in waves—some hours are okay, but others I just want to curl up and cry.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah... it's happened a few times this week. Yesterday I just sat in the nursery rocking chair with the baby finally asleep on me, and I felt this wave of sadness hit. I couldn't stop the tears—I had to bite my lip so I wouldn't wake him up. Sometimes it feels like the tears come out of nowhere, even when nothing specific happened.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, I haven’t had any thoughts like that. I’m exhausted and overwhelmed, but I’d never want to leave my baby or hurt myself—he needs me.

You've shared how the joy of new motherhood feels clouded by daily <sym>sadness</sym>, constant <sym>worry</sym>, and a sense of being overwhelmed. Despite loving your baby, most activities now feel like chores, laughter is fleeting, and you often blame yourself when things go wrong. Nights are restless, mornings feel heavy, and you've found yourself crying unexpectedly.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports diminished enjoyment and spontaneity of laughter; it now feels forced and short-lived, aligning with 'definitely not so much now'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports almost complete loss of anticipatory joy, describing dread or emotional flatness even for small positive events, aligning with "Hardly at all".</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blame "a lot," links baby's fussing to her feeding or timing mistakes, ruminates on perceived failures, and concludes other moms manage while she fails—clearly "most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports near-daily, intrusive, physiologically intense anxiety without identifiable triggers</sym>, <sym>Patient describes classic panic attack (sudden breathlessness, shaking, derealisation) occurring multiple times without trigger, matching "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily overwhelm, inability to keep up, and feeling paralyzed—matching "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all".</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly racing thoughts, prolonged sleep onset (>1 hr), and hyper-arousal to baby sounds, indicating sleep difficulty "most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports sadness "most mornings" and "in waves," matching "Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient confirms crying several times in the week and describes sudden, intense episodes; this aligns with "Yes, quite often."</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS scoring places you well above the 14-point cutoff for probable major <med>postpartum depression</med>, with peak scores on core mood items (Q2,3,8) and anxiety items (Q4,5). Your descriptions map onto <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: markedly diminished interest or pleasure, inappropriate guilt, psychomotor agitation observed as restless scanning, insomnia, fatigue, and recurrent tearfulness. <quote>I'm too tired or worried to find things genuinely funny</quote> and <quote>I wake up most mornings feeling heavy</quote> exemplify these symptoms. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or perinatal mental-health team
2. Discuss starting evidence-based treatment such as <med>CBT</med>, an <med>SSRI</med>, or both
3. Ask partner or family to alternate night feeds so you can obtain 4-6 hrs of uninterrupted sleep
4. Schedule brief daily walks or gentle exercise; proven to reduce <sym>depressive symptoms</sym>
5. Connect with local postpartum support group or online communities
6. Use 5-minute breathing or grounding exercises when you notice <sym>panic sensations</sym>
7. Plan a follow-up EPDS in two weeks to monitor progress
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening – 2–3 wk post-delivery  
Source: self-report EPDS-style questionnaire

Areas endorsed (clinically significant):
- Anhedonia / low mood: diminished capacity for pleasure, “forced” laughter, absence of anticipatory enjoyment (Q1, Q2)
- Excessive guilt / self-blame: attributes infant fussing to maternal failure; repetitive rumination (Q3)
- Generalized & situation-specific anxiety: daily “scanning” for hazards, racing heart; at least one acute panic episode with dyspnea and trembling while bottle-warming (Q4, Q5)
- Overwhelm / impaired coping: feeling paralyzed by household tasks; difficulty sequencing or completing chores (Q6)
- Sleep disturbance: initial insomnia, hypervigilant awakenings despite infant sleep; fatigue compounding mood symptoms (Q7)
- Persistent sadness & crying spells: “gray cloud,” tearfulness without clear trigger; guilt over “not bubbling with joy” (Q8, Q9)
- Suicidality: denied (Q10)

Risk factors noted: primiparous status, high self-expectations, sleep deprivation, absence of practical support described.

Protective factors: strong infant attachment, no self-harm ideation, motivated to seek help.

Screening impression: elevated depressive and anxiety symptoms consistent with probable postpartum depression ± comorbid anxiety; no immediate safety concerns. Recommend formal clinical interview (EPDS/PHQ-9) and referral for perinatal mental health evaluation.
